text.p: Austrian research body Wifo said on Monday it raised its 1996 forecast for Austrian inflation to as much as 1.9 percent from a previous estimate of 1.7 percent following the release of worse-than-expected inflation data.
"We have to up our forecast to 1.8 or 1.9 percent for the year," Wolfgang Pollan of Wifo, whose studies form the basis for the Austrian government's economic policy, told Reuters.

The central statistics office earlier on Monday said year-on-year inflation rose to a one-year peak of two percent in September, up from 1.8 percent in August. September prices were down 0.8 percent from a month earlier.
Pollan said inflation could exceed two percent over the next few months unless energy prices retreated and the effects of moderate wage deals filtered through.
The central statistics office blamed the rise in September inflation on higher energy prices after recent gains in crude oil prices as well as higher rent and fruit prices.
Heating costs alone were up 6.8 percent in September from a year ago, the office said.
Austrian petrol prices were raised by some 0.2 schillings per litre over the past month as crude oil prices hit a six-year high last week.

Much of Austria's star performance on the inflation front over the past year has been attributed to its membership of the European Union, which led to lower prices primarily in the once-sheltered food sector.

Austria joined the EU in January 1995, and for much of the past year was among the group's top-three inflation performers. The September figures have relegated Austria to eighth place, just behind Belgium and a notch ahead of Britain.

The Austrian electorate last week delivered a stark protest vote to the governing coalition of Social Democrats and conservatives, giving the far-right Freedom Party its best nationwide result in the country's first European Parliament elections.

Analysts traced the result to growing disaffection with the EU over smaller-than-promised price declines and increased belt-tightening designed to make the country fit for Europe's planned economic and monetary union.
